title: Eighty-seven years, 30 moments
lede: From a candy wholesaler in the Berkshires to a trademark that has changed hands three times since the stores closed. Filter by thread.

events.title: Kaufman Brothers founded
events.text: Harry and Joseph Kaufman start a candy company in Pittsfield, Massachusetts.

events.title: From candy to toys
events.text: With sugar scarce in wartime, the brothers begin to switch to toys, and later drop confectionery.

events.title: Wholesaling ends
events.text: The company gives up wholesale to run its 26 retail stores as Kay-Bee Toy & Hobby.

events.title: Sold to Melville Corporation
events.text: Kay-Bee has 210 stores. A reference history gives the price as $64.2 million.

events.title: Melville buys Circus World
events.text: The 330-store chain, with 1989 sales of $177.6 million, is to become part of the Kay-Bee division.

events.title: Nearly 250 stores closed
events.text: A restructuring closes weaker stores. In 1994 Kay-Bee starts larger Toy Works stores outside malls.

events.title: Melville agrees to sell
events.text: Consolidated Stores will pay $315 million: $215 million in cash and a $100 million note.

events.title: Consolidated takes over
events.text: The acquisition is effective. Kay-Bee operates 1,042 stores. A later adjustment cuts the cash paid to $185.3 million.

events.title: The peak: 1,322 stores
events.text: 974 of them are in enclosed malls. Fiscal 1998 toy sales are $1,643.0 million, with comparable sales down 0.2%.

events.title: The BrainPlay deal
events.text: Consolidated says it will invest $80 million in a web venture with BrainPlay.com and own 80% of it.

events.title: KBkids.com LLC formed
events.text: Consolidated contributes $80 million of cash and intangibles valued at $4 million.

events.title: A profit warning
events.text: Consolidated warns of a quarterly loss, citing slow video game sales at KB. Its shares fall nearly 30% in a day.

events.title: KBkids.com files to go public
events.text: The planned offering is $210 million, under the symbol KBKD.

events.title: The web chief is fired
events.text: Consolidated dismisses the head of KBkids.com and 50 of the unit’s other 150 employees.

events.title: IPO withdrawn
events.text: KBkids.com pulls the $210 million offering.

events.title: The toy division is put up for sale
events.text: Consolidated announces it will separate its toy and closeout businesses.

events.title: Sold to Bain Capital and management
events.text: Gross proceeds are about $305 million. Consolidated records a $430.8 million after-tax loss on disposal.

events.title: eToys inventory bought
events.text: KB agrees to pay about $5.4 million for inventory of the bankrupt web retailer [eToys](/etoys/).

events.title: KB Toys at Sears
events.text: Sears says it will test holiday toy shops run with KB in 29 department stores.

events.title: The recapitalization
events.text: KB takes on $66 million of bank loans to fund an $85 million payment to Bain, as reported by Forbes. A court later describes about $120 million distributed in all.

events.title: The holiday price war
events.text: Discounters sell hot toys below wholesale cost. KB’s comparable sales fall 10% for the year. FAO Inc. files for Chapter 11.

events.title: First Chapter 11
events.text: KB files for bankruptcy protection. USA Today counts 1,217 stores.

events.title: At least 375 stores to close
events.text: KB says it will cut 3,500 jobs. Clearance sales begin at the first 356 stores.

events.title: Out of bankruptcy
events.text: KB announces it has emerged, with 640 stores, a Prentice Capital affiliate as majority owner and Gregory Staley as chief executive.

events.title: The seller’s lawsuit is dismissed
events.text: A Delaware judge dismisses all counts of Big Lots’ suit against Bain and former KB executives.

events.title: 156 more stores targeted
events.text: The Washington Post reports the closures from internal documents. KB has fewer than 600 stores.

events.title: Second Chapter 11, to liquidate
events.text: Comparable sales are down 20% since October 5. Going-out-of-business sales start at once.

events.title: Toys “R” Us buys the name
events.text: The brand, KBToys.com and trademarks go to a Toys “R” Us subsidiary. No stores are included.

events.title: The trademark lapses and is re-registered
events.text: Toys “R” Us lets the registration expire in June. Strategic Marks picks it up in December.

events.title: A comeback is announced
events.text: Strategic Marks plans 1,000 pop-up stores for the holidays. By March 2019 none had opened.
